title: Beads of prayer
hook: counting prayers on beads grew in the middle ages; the Orthodox use knotted prayer ropes

segments.voice: Yesterday, pilgrims' roads to Rome, Santiago and Canterbury. Your line was the road is the prayer. Where did your walk take you? Day eight hundred forty-three.

A grandmother's hands, folded in her lap, with a loop of beads running through her fingers. Her lips move. Every few seconds, her thumb slides one bead along. In another house, in another church, a monk holds a loop of black wool, tied in thick knots, and his thumb moves the same way. Bead, word. Knot, word. Neither of them is looking at their hands. The hands are keeping count so the heart doesn't have to. Today: beads of prayer.
screen: `A LOOP OF BEADS IN HER FINGERS.`

segments.voice: Christians counting prayers is an old habit. Tradition remembers desert monks who counted their prayers with pebbles, moving one stone from one pile to another. Later, in the West, people threaded beads on a string to count the Lord's Prayer, the Our Father, again and again. In the middle ages these strings grew into the rosary, where Catholics pray the Hail Mary in sets, each set beginning with the Our Father, while they think about scenes from the lives of Jesus and Mary. In the East, Orthodox monks use a prayer rope, a loop of wool knotted again and again, and with each knot they say the Jesus Prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me. Orthodox monks tell a story about it. A holy monk tied knots in a cord to count his prayers, and the devil kept untying them. So the monk learned to tie each knot as a little web of crosses, and the devil couldn't undo them. Whatever its origin, the story says something true about how these ropes are meant: each knot is made to hold. Why repeat a prayer at all? Paul tells one church, in the King James Bible, "Pray without ceasing." Repetition is one way people have tried to obey that line. But Jesus also says, in Matthew, "use not vain repetitions." Some Protestants are cautious about counted prayers for that reason, and pray in their own words. Catholic and Orthodox teachers answer that a prayer said from the heart isn't vain, however often it's said. Each side reads the same Gospel seriously.
screen: `BEADS FOR THE OUR FATHER, THEN THE ROSARY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: count ten prayers on your fingers. Rest your hands in your lap. Choose one short line. If you pray, it might be the Jesus Prayer, or the first line of the Our Father, or a line from a Psalm. If you don't, it might be a single word like thanks, or the name of someone you love. Touch your thumb to one fingertip and say the line, slowly. Then the next fingertip. Ten times, across both hands. If you lose count, start again without fuss. The bell holds the time.
Jesus Prayer. The words Orthodox monks repeat on a knotted prayer rope, Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, so the hands keep count and the heart can pray.
Your line: counting love. Today, count ten good things about someone who's hard to love, one finger at a time, before you speak to them. Day eight hundred forty-three.

howItsDone: Catholics pray the rosary on a string of beads, alone or together, and Orthodox Christians pray the Jesus Prayer on a knotted prayer rope; some Anglicans and Lutherans use prayer beads too.

what a scholar hears: desert monks' pebbles, paternoster strings, the rosary, the Orthodox prayer rope, and the debate over Matthew 6:7.

notes: Claims rule: no counts (number of beads, knots or Hail Marys) or dates are given. Protestant caution is phrased as 'some Protestants'.
Desert monk counting prayers with pebbles: Palladius, Lausiac History (Paul of Pherme); given as 'tradition remembers'. Confirm.
Paternoster beads in the West, growth of the rosary in the middle ages: standard; confirm summary.
Prayer rope legend (often attributed to Pachomius): labeled a story, not a record. Confirm.
Jesus Prayer quoted in its common form (a traditional prayer, not a new one).

Matthew 6:7 quoted only in part ('use not vain repetitions'); the full verse continues 'as the heathen do', omitted to avoid a contrast with another tradition. Confirm the omission is fair to the text.
howItsDone: Anglican and Lutheran prayer beads (e.g. the Anglican rosary, the Pearls of Life): confirm.
